report.headline: Usage projected to fall from 17.8% to 14.4% in the NBA; shooting efficiency projection carries no information

projection.text: Modeled usage rate in the NBA is 14.4%, down from a 17.8% share of possessions in the 2016-17 G League season, placing the projection about one standard deviation below the NBA's 20.1% average usage rate (sd 5.2%).

risks.text: The projected true shooting percentage of 51.8% should not be trusted: its out-of-fold error of 4.7% is no better than the 4.7% error of simply predicting the league mean, meaning this number carries no real signal beyond that baseline.
The usage estimate rests on only 45 historical G League to NBA transitions, a fairly thin cohort to generalize from.
Source-season indicators were mixed: a 16.9% turnover rate alongside a below-average standardized usage rate of -0.46 sd within the G League.

strengths.text: The usage projection is trustworthy relative to a naive guess: its out-of-fold error of 3.3% beats the best trivial baseline's 4.3% error for usage rate.
Players who made this G League to NBA transition historically sat about +0.27 standard deviations above their own league's average, and this player fits that selection profile as a mover.
Source-season production included 13.819 points, 3.014 assists, and 13.182 rebounds per 75 possessions, with a 12.4% assist rate.

uncertainty.text: The 80% prediction interval for usage runs from 9.2% to 19.7%, a span of roughly two standard deviations of NBA usage rate, and the 95% interval widens further to 6.4%-22.5%; the model can rank this player against peers but cannot pin down an individual value.
